title: Writing icons
hookLine: iconographers pray and fast as they paint

lines: A WHITE BOARD, AN EGG, A CUP OF WATER.
cards: A small room, early morning. A wooden board, coated smooth and white. Beside it, jars of colored powder, an egg, a cup of water, brushes.
The painter hasn't eaten breakfast, and won't until the day's work is done. Before touching a brush, they stand, make the sign of the cross, and pray.
Then they begin, not with a blank idea, but with a pattern handed down for this exact face. One line, then another. The finished face will hang in a church or a home, with candles lit before it.
Orthodox Christians have a particular word for this. They don't always call it painting.

teach.h: AN ICON IS READ, LIKE A PAGE.
teach.b: Some Orthodox Christians speak of writing an icon rather than painting one, because an icon is read, like a page.
Its faces, hands, colors and gestures follow patterns passed down from earlier icons, so the iconographer isn't inventing a new look for a saint.
They're copying a text faithfully, the way a scribe copies a Gospel: handing something on, not showing off a style.

teach.h: PRAYER AND FASTING AT THE BOARD.
teach.b: Next, the prayer. Tradition says the iconographer prays before and during the work, and some keep a fast. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his listeners to fast quietly, not for show.
An icon is made in that spirit, traditionally without a signature: the hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Then, why pictures at all. Back in year three, the icon wars turned on this.
Orthodox Christians point to John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Once God has a human face, that face can be painted.

Some Protestant churches keep their walls bare, reading the commandment in Exodus: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Each side takes that text seriously, and reads it differently. Last, the craftsman.
In Exodus, God names an artisan, Bezalel: "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship."
Skill with the hands, counted as a gift of the spirit. Iconographers stand in that line.

how: In Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, iconographers traditionally pray before and during their work, may keep a fast, and follow patterns handed down for each saint; the finished icons are blessed and placed in churches and homes for prayer.

games.q: you're an iconographer, about to begin a face of Christ on a fresh white board. how do you start?
o: sketch freely, in your own new style.
pray, and follow the pattern handed down.
copy a photograph of a model.
games.why: tradition says the iconographer prays first and follows the old pattern. the aim is to hand something on faithfully, not to invent.

practice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, draw one simple thing in front of you, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, so slowly that each line takes a full breath, with no erasing and no judging. The point is attention, not a good drawing.
If you pray, you can pray before the first line, the way an iconographer does; if you don't, let the slowness itself be the practice.

wordCard.voice: Writing icons. Making a holy image in prayer and fasting, following patterns handed down, so it can be read like a page.

carryVoice: Your line: painting as prayer. The hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Back tomorrow, same hill.
